phonemes.desc: Voiceless glottal [h] plus short high [i]; the unstressed opening syllable, light as breath.
The glottal stop [ʔ] written ʻokina, followed by the long vowel ī [iː] that carries the Hawaiian stress.
Open [a] and the velar stop plus [a]; the unstressed close, quick and even.

pronunciation.approximation: 'hee-EE-ah-kah' — four light syllables, the second long and stressed; give the doubled i a tiny catch in the throat (the ʻokina).

kin.label: Hawaiian
kin.form: hiʻi, 'to hold or carry a child in the arms or on the hip' — the name Hiʻiaka is traditionally read 'carried at the bosom' (Pukui & Elbert, Hawaiian Dictionary; Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology)

kin.label: Hawaiian
kin.form: aka, 'shadow, reflection' — a second traditional parsing, 'bosom shadow'; the philology is remembered rather than certain

kin.label: The Pele family
kin.form: Kāmohoaliʻi and Kāne-milo-hai, her brothers; Pele-honua-mea, her sister — the volcano household of the Pele cycle

pronunciation.note: Hiiaka is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized form is plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter to recover. The fuller Hawaiian spelling Hiʻiaka carries both the ʻokina, a true consonant the ASCII erases, and the long ī. The temple keeps the normalized restoration and shows the fuller form in the lore.

domains.title: Hiiaka
domains.subtitle: Hula
domains.lead: Hiiaka is the youngest sister of the volcano-goddess Pele: patroness of the hula, guardian of the hālau hula where the dance is taught, and a healer whose chants restore the dying. Her story — an oath, a quest, and a betrayal between sisters — is the great romance of the Hawaiian Pele cycle.

cards.name: Sacred Name
cards.desc: The restoration Hiiaka names the goddess Hawaiʻi's dancers invoke before any performance begins.

cards.name: Hula
cards.desc: She is patroness of the hālau hula and keeper of the mele and dances taught to her friend Hopoe at Puna.

cards.name: Healing Chant
cards.desc: Her repertoire includes the chants (mele oli) that raise the dying — the power she finally spends on Lohiʻau.

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: The fuller Hawaiian form is Hiʻiaka, with ʻokina and long ī; the normalized Hiiaka keeps the name registrable.

symbols.name: The egg at ʻĀinahou
symbols.meaning: Her first form, found on Kauaʻi and warmed in Pele's bosom until the goddess hatched — the birth the name Hiʻiaka ('carried at the bosom') remembers

symbols.name: The pāʻū hula
symbols.meaning: The dancer's skirt, emblem of her office as patroness of the hula schools

symbols.name: The ʻōhiʻa lehua
symbols.meaning: The red blossom of Puna beneath which her friend Hopoe danced — the groves she swore to protect

symbols.name: Mele oli
symbols.meaning: The unaccompanied chant through which her healing power works, restoring breath and life

symbols.name: The kupua's path
symbols.meaning: The road across the islands she fought along — passes guarded by moʻo serpents that she cleared for every traveler after

mythology.lead: Hiiaka's mythology is the longest continuous narrative in Hawaiian tradition: the Pele cycle, preserved in chant and family memory, in which the youngest volcano-goddess crosses every island on her sister's errand and comes home to a betrayal that splits the heavens' first family in two.

myths.title: The Egg at ʻĀinahou
myths.text:
Pele's migration legend carries the volcano family westward from Kahiki — the Hawaiian name for Tahiti — until the goddess finds her home in the pit of Kīlauea. Beckwith's digest of the tradition (Hawaiian Mythology, 'The Pele cycle') preserves the birth of her youngest sister: at ʻĀinahou on Kauaʻi, Pele discovers an egg and takes it into her bosom to keep it warm; from the egg hatches the goddess whose name, Hiʻiaka, is traditionally explained as 'carried in the bosom' (Hawaiian hiʻi, to hold a child close; Pukui & Elbert, Hawaiian Dictionary).

The myth makes kinship the first fact of Hiʻiaka's being: she exists because Pele carried her, and her whole career will replay that carrying as loyalty, as errand, and finally as grievance.

myths.title: The Quest for Lohiʻau
myths.text:
Sleeping in the crater at Kīlauea, Pele sees in a dream the young chief Lohiʻau of Kauaʻi and falls in love with his image. Because she cannot leave her volcanic work without peril, she binds her youngest sister by an oath: Hiʻiaka must cross the islands, find Lohiʻau, and bring him back within forty days — and Hiʻiaka in turn binds Pele to guard her sacred lehua groves and her beloved friend Hopoe until she returns (Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology; Emerson's Pele and Hiiaka, 1915, is the classic literary retelling of the cycle).

The journey becomes the longest road in Hawaiian myth: Hiʻiaka battles the moʻo monsters that bar the passes, wins kupua allies of her own, and at last finds Lohiʻau dead of longing — and slays the serpent who killed him, passing her pāʻū over his body until he breathes again. The quest myth turns the islands into a single moral geography: every valley crossed is a test of the oath, and love in this family is always love at the end of a long and dangerous errand.

myths.title: The Death of Hopoe
myths.text:
Hiʻiaka's double charge was the lehua groves and Hopoe, the dancer-friend of her girlhood at Puna. When the fortieth day passed with no sister on the road home, Pele's jealousy did what her fire always does: the lava took the groves, and it took Hopoe. Beckwith records the scene as the Puna coast's own aetiology — the dancer caught by the advancing flow at the shore — and later tellers of the cycle say her dance was fixed in the stone where the wave of lava stopped.

Hiʻiaka, racing home with Lohiʻau alive, found her friend dead and her groves burned by the very goddess she had sworn to serve. The myth builds its tragedy on crossed oaths: Pele broke the pledge her sister trusted most, and the volcano-goddess's oldest excuse — that fire cannot help itself — is asked to answer for a deliberate grief.

myths.title: Sister Against Sister
myths.text:
When Hiʻiaka reached home and found Hopoe dead, she broke the last restraint: she embraced Lohiʻau before Pele's altar — the final insult in the sisters' escalating war — and Pele's answer was to burn Lohiʻau where he stood and open the earth under Hiʻiaka. The battle that followed, along the Hilo and Puna coasts, set the two sisters' powers against one another until their brothers, led by Kāmohoaliʻi the shark-god, forced a peace (Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology). Hiʻiaka's last labor in the cycle is her descent to the spirit-realm of Lua-o-Milu, whence she brings Lohiʻau's soul back and restores him by her own power.

The Pele cycle ends not with victory but with partition: each sister keeps her domain — the fire and the dance, the volcano and the healing chant — and Hawaiian tradition thereafter treats them as one household's two halves, destruction and restoration, both of them family.

lore.syncretism: The Pele cycle in which Hiʻiaka moves is itself a layered composition: Hawaiian tradition remembers the family's arrival from Kahiki (Tahiti), and Beckwith read the migration of the volcano deities against Tahitian parallels, while the offices of hula and healing chant root the goddess in religion older than any remembered voyage. Nineteenth-century Christianity nearly silenced the cycle: missionaries suppressed the hula after the 1820s, and the chants survived only inside the hālau lineages and a few manuscripts, of which Emerson's Pele and Hiiaka (1915) is the great published monument. The modern Hawaiian renaissance returned both the dance and its goddess to public honor.
lore.culturalLegacy: Hālau hula across Hawaiʻi still open their practice with chants to Pele and Hiʻiaka, and the Merrie Monarch Festival's hula competition, founded in 1964 and held each spring in Hilo — the very coast of the sisters' battle — is the visible heart of her cult today. Place memory keeps her close: ʻĀinahou on Kauaʻi where the egg lay, the groves and shores of Puna where Hopoe danced. In the Hawaiian renaissance her name has returned to concert stages, children's books, and mele, and to the recovery of the ʻōlelo Hawaiʻi in which her chants were always sung.
lore.extendedMeditation: Hiʻiaka is the myth of loyalty tested by power. She is the youngest, the carried one, the sister whose gifts — dance, chant, healing — are the gentle arts, and the story gives her the one role the gentle arts dread: the enforcer of another's desire. Her oath to Pele sends her across an ocean of islands to kill monsters and raise the dead; and the same oath ends with her friend burned and her own goddess against her. The myth's wisdom is that devotion and obedience are not the same, and that the hearth that raised you can also demand what it has no right to burn. Every hālau that chants to her chooses the gentler half of that lesson: serve the love, not the fire.

lore.archaeology: Pre-contact Hawaiʻi had no writing, so Hiʻiaka's evidence is cultic and ethnographic rather than epigraphic. The material center of her family's worship is the pit of Kīlauea: nineteenth-century observers (Emerson, Westervelt) and native historians (Kamakau, Malo) record offerings of ʻōhelo berries and lehua blossom at Halemaʻumaʻu, where the Pele family was believed to dwell. The chants of the cycle were preserved in the memory of the hālau and committed to manuscript in the nineteenth century; Emerson's Pele and Hiiaka (1915) drew directly on that living tradition. Heiau dedicated to the Pele family along the Puna and Kaʻū coasts, many now reduced to stone platforms, mark the old geography of the cycle's events.
lore.originalScriptNote: Pre-contact Hawaiʻi had no writing; the name comes down in the Latin-based Hawaiian orthography developed after the 1820s. The fuller traditional spelling is Hiʻiaka, with ʻokina (glottal stop) marking the consonant between the vowels and kahakō (macron) marking the long ī; the canonical temple restoration is the normalized form Hiiaka.
